extracted.intended_audience: students, lawyers, policy practitioners, regulated parties, and members of the public interested in administrative rulemaking (particularly U.S. federal rulemaking)
extracted.subtask_description: High-level explanatory guidance on the U.S. (and comparative) administrative rulemaking process, including statutory and procedural standards for notice, comment, analysis, recordkeeping, and judicial review. Useful for people who need to understand how agency rules are proposed, reviewed, and challenged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public notice and opportunity to comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The public is informed of proposed rules before they take effect; the public can comment on the proposed rules and provide additional data to the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proposed rule is published in the Federal Register and a public comment period begins (commonly 30 to 180 days depending on complexity). Most agencies are required to respond to every issue raised in comments. Public comments become part of the rulemaking record and are central to public participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking record and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency creates a permanent record of its analysis and the process; agencies must assemble and make public a rulemaking record that includes all information considered as part of the rulemaking process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records can be large (scores to hundreds of boxes). Interested parties frequently inspect the record to find flaws. The federal government is moving toward posting dockets online at regulations.gov; supporting documentation availability increased from 37% (2006) to 80% (2007) for new rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must analyze and respond to public comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency analyzes and responds to the public's comments; in the final rule the agency publishes a full response to issues raised by public comments and an updated analysis and justification for the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses should address issues raised and incorporate or analyze any new data submitted by the public. If a final rule is substantially different, the agency may publish a second proposed rule to allow fresh public comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation with the public before Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) / required evaluation factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Before publication in a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, the agency must 'consult with members of the public' to evaluate: (i) whether the proposed collection of information is necessary; (ii) the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden; (iii) how to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and (iv) minimize the burden of the collection on respondents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consultation is practically necessary to produce 'objectively supported' burden estimates for OMB submissions; it often requires conferring with stakeholders (e.g., attorneys who do similar work) sufficiently in advance of the NPRM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction / OMB information-collection submission requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rule that imposes or modifies any 'information collection' burden on the public must be submitted to the Director of OMB with 'objectively supported' estimates no later than the time of a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As part of the submission, the agency must certify or demonstrate that the information collection: (a) is necessary for proper performance of agency functions; (b) is not unnecessarily duplicative of information already accessible to the agency; (c) the agency has taken every reasonable step to ensure the proposed collection is the least burdensome necessary; and (d) the regulations are 'written using plain, coherent, and unambiguous terminology.' (Citations: 44 U.S.C. §§ 3506, 3507; 5 C.F.R. parts referenced in article.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Impact Analysis for economically significant rules (EO 12866 / OMB Circular A-4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the rule is 'economically significant' under Executive Order 12,866, the agency must prepare a Regulatory Impact Analysis under OMB Circular A-4 before publishing an NPRM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive Order 12,866 defines 'significant regulatory action' (e.g., $100M+ effect on economy; materially alter budgets/rights; raise novel legal or policy issues). The RIA is required to support cost-benefit balancing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of proposed rule with supporting justification
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Proposed Rule step, the agency publishes the actual proposed regulatory language in the Federal Register along with a discussion of the justification and analysis behind the rule, and the agency's response to any public comment on any advance notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication must include sufficient explanation and analysis to allow meaningful public comment and to support later judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) and negotiated rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: An ANPRM is an optional step publishing the agency's initial analysis and often asking for early public input; negotiated rulemaking convenes a board of affected parties to negotiate rule terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ANPRMs make data and communications available for review and can be an opportunity to collect needed information. Negotiated rulemaking can produce more custom-tailored proposals and reduce deadlock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final rule content and mid-process revision (second proposed rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually the proposed rule becomes final with minor modifications; in the Final Rule the agency publishes a full response to issues raised and updated analysis. If the final rule is so different that it raises new issues, the agency may publish a second proposed rule to allow comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must analyze any new data submitted during comment and explain changes. Failure to allow comment on materially new provisions can give rise to judicial relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date timing and 'good cause' exception
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States a final rule is generally effective no less than thirty days after publication in the Federal Register; the agency may make a rule effective sooner only by citing 'good cause' why immediate effectiveness is in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant rules (EO 12866) and major rules (SBREFA) are required to have a 60-day delayed effective date. Courts may scrutinize claims of 'good cause.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid rulemaking constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Hybrid' rulemaking (between formal and informal) is not a legal term of art; hybrid features (e.g., a formal hearing with sworn testimony and cross-examination) are proper only when specifically provided for by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory construction of the APA and the Supreme Court's Vermont Yankee decision limit hybrid procedures unless Congress authorizes them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review standard — arbitrary and capricious / unsupported by the record
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain court-ordered changes in a rule, a party must argue the rule is arbitrary and capricious and/or unsupported by the administrative record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts defer to agency expertise on technical matters but will intervene if there's an obvious gap in the agency's data or analysis or if no reasonable way exists that the agency could have drafted the rule given the record. A court remand usually results in additional notice and public comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review standard — exceeds statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts will review whether the regulation exceeds the rulemaking authority granted by the authorizing legislation; rules may be invalidated if they fail to follow instructions of authorizing statutes (too strict or too lax).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if a law instructs an agency to ban a chemical but the agency instead sets safe-use levels, a court may order a new rule consistent with the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review standard — 'bolt out of the blue' (new, unvetted provisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may intervene if a final rule contains provisions that were never vetted during the public comment period such that the public could not have anticipated them and provided comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies commonly vet several options during the proposed rule phase to allow comment on the full spectrum. Introducing truly new provisions in the final rule risks invalidation or remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) as governing law
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrative Procedure Act is the primary governing law for U.S. federal rulemaking; it imposes standards of due process, notice-and-comment, and judicially enforceable procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State systems often have parallel statutes; Commonwealth countries use a mix of common law and statute. APA requirements underlie many of the procedural criteria listed in this article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and executive instruments that constrain rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple statutes and executive instruments constrain agency rulemaking, including: the Housekeeping Act (authority for agency internal rules), Regulatory Flexibility Act (consider needs of small entities), Paperwork Reduction Act (limits on information collection), Congressional Review Act (Congressional review/veto), Independent Offices Appropriations Act (limits on user fees), and Executive Order 12866 (cost-benefit balancing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each instrument imposes specific obligations (e.g., RFA requires consideration of small entities; PRA requires OMB review of information collections; CRA allows Congress to review and potentially disapprove rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public participation apparatus and official publication channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must use official methods to communicate with the public—usually publication in an official gazette such as the Federal Register; final rule language is codified in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accountability assumes the public notices Federal Register entries; in practice industry groups or advocates often monitor and disseminate notices on behalf of constituencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scientific, economic, and industry expertise and flexibility in delegated rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking serves to add scientific, economic, or industry expertise and implementation detail to broad legislative mandates, allowing for nuanced approaches, updating as new data/technology emerges, and finding compromise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: FDA standards for lab tests under FDCA; EPA industry-by-industry emissions technologies under the Clean Air/Clean Water Acts; delegation permits more easily changeable standards than statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies must use plain, coherent, and unambiguous terminology for regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations (and submissions to OMB regarding information collection) must be 'written using plain, coherent, and unambiguous terminology.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement supports clarity for respondents and for judicial review; it is tied to Paperwork Reduction Act/OIRA information-collection certification obligations.
